opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The glass example is one I come back to a lot, because it sounds trivial and it's not. A two-year-old can walk up to a table and pick up a glass they've never seen before, a wine glass, a tumbler, a plastic cup, maybe half-full of water, and do it reliably on the first try. For a robot, that's still remarkably hard. It's a nice everyday illustration of Moravec's paradox: the things we find effortless, like perception and manipulation, are the things machines find hardest, while the things we find hard, like chess or calculus, have turned out to be comparatively easy for computers.

So why does the way humans do it matter? A few reasons.

First, look at what's going on when you reach for that glass. You're not computing a precise 3D model and then executing a perfect trajectory. You're dealing with enormous uncertainty: you don't know the exact weight, the friction of the surface, whether it's wet, where the center of mass is if there's liquid sloshing around. Glass is also transparent, which is a nightmare for depth cameras. And yet we handle all of that gracefully. That tells us robustness doesn't come from eliminating uncertainty. It comes from strategies that tolerate it.

Second, humans use contact and feedback constantly. Watch someone closely and you'll see they often make contact with the table or slide their fingers around the glass, adjusting as they go. We're using touch, compliance in our skin and joints, and small corrections in real time. A lot of early robot grasping was very open-loop: plan a grasp, close the gripper, hope for the best. Thinking about how humans do it pushes you toward closed-loop, contact-rich strategies, and toward compliant hardware that absorbs errors instead of amplifying them.

Third, it's a reminder of how much humans generalize. We have a kind of intuitive physics: we know a glass can tip, that it's fragile, that we should grip it lower if it's full. That's built from a lifetime of experience. When we worked on Dex-Net, part of the idea was to give robots something analogous: train on huge numbers of synthetic objects with physics models and noise built in, so the robot learns grasps that are robust across uncertainty rather than optimal for one idealized case.

And honestly, it's a source of humility. There's a lot of excitement right now about humanoid robots and the idea that they'll be in our homes doing chores very soon. I'm optimistic about progress, but when you really study something as simple as picking up a glass, you appreciate how much is happening under the hood, and how far we still have to go. I think the gap between what robots can do in a demo and what they can do reliably in messy real environments is still large. Taking human manipulation seriously helps us be honest about that gap and points us toward what we actually need: better sensing, especially touch, better hardware, and a mix of learning and good old-fashioned engineering and physics, rather than assuming data alone will solve it.

r001.rationale: The response describes human corrections and robot grasping challenges, but does not identify susceptibility to manipulation errors as a limitation shared by both.

r002.rationale: It mentions sliding fingers around the glass and adjusting, but does not explain a scooping motion or how finger closure compensates for small positioning errors.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. The reason I keep coming back to the glass is that it exposes a gap most people don't notice. When you reach for a glass of water, you don't compute anything. You don't measure the diameter, you don't estimate the coefficient of friction, you don't worry about where exactly your fingers land. You just reach out, and it works, essentially every time. If the glass is a little further than you thought, or wet, or someone bumped the table, your hand adjusts without you ever being aware of it.

Robots are the opposite. For decades we've approached grasping as a precision problem. You build a very accurate model of the object, you compute the exact contact points that give you force closure, and then you execute that plan. And it works beautifully in simulation. The problem is that reality never matches the model. The camera is off by a few millimeters, the object isn't quite where you think it is, the gripper closes a little late. And a plan that was optimal for the idealized glass fails completely on the real one.

So what the human example tells me is that robustness doesn't come from being precise. It comes from being tolerant of imprecision. Humans have evolved strategies, often without knowing it, that work under uncertainty. We tend to grasp things in ways where being off by a centimeter doesn't matter. We use the environment, we slide along the table, we let the object settle into our hand. We rely on compliance in our fingers and skin rather than exact positioning.

That reframing has been central to a lot of what my lab has done. Instead of asking what is the single best grasp for this object, we ask which grasps are most likely to succeed given that we don't know the object's exact shape, pose, or friction. You end up preferring grasps that look a little boring, centered on a flat face, deep in the gripper, because they have a large margin for error. That's what Dex-Net was really about: learning to predict grasp robustness under uncertainty rather than grasp optimality.

And I think there's a broader lesson in it. People sometimes watch a toddler pick up a cup and think manipulation must be easy because a two-year-old can do it. I'd flip that. The fact that a toddler can do it, with no explicit knowledge of physics, after millions of years of evolution tuning the hand and the nervous system, suggests the problem is extraordinarily hard and that the solution is deeply tied to handling variability. If we want robots that work in a kitchen or a warehouse rather than a lab, that's the capability we actually have to build.

r001.rationale: The response says humans adjust to small changes while robots often fail when their models are inaccurate; it does not identify susceptibility to manipulation errors as a shared limitation.

r002.rationale: The response mentions sliding along the table and compliant fingers, but does not explain a scooping motion around the glass or how finger closure compensates for positioning errors.

astra-6.text:
Picking up a glass looks simple, but it involves a remarkable amount of adaptation. You don’t know its exact position, its weight, or how slippery the surface is. You reach toward it, make contact, and adjust. If it starts to slip, you change your grip. You’re using feedback throughout the action.

That’s important for robotics because a robot’s model of the world is always imperfect. Its camera gives it an estimate of where the glass is, and its motions have some uncertainty too. If the grasp only works when everything is exactly where the robot expects it to be, it’s going to be brittle.

So the question is: can we design a grasp that succeeds across a range of possible positions and conditions, and then use feedback to correct as we go? The glass is an everyday example, but it gets right to the central challenge: making manipulation work reliably in a world we can’t measure or predict perfectly.

r001.rationale: The response describes humans adapting to uncertainty about the glass and robots facing imperfect models and motion uncertainty, conveying that both are vulnerable to manipulation errors.

r002.rationale: It mentions reaching, contact, and adjustment, but does not explain that a scooping motion lets finger closure compensate for small positioning errors.

sol-6.1.text:
Think about picking up a glass. It feels almost trivial, but you don’t know its exact position, its weight, or how slippery the surface is. Your visual estimate is imperfect. And yet you reach out, make contact, and adjust. You don’t need a perfect model of the glass before you can act.

That’s important for robotics because uncertainty is always there. The object isn’t exactly where the camera says it is, and the friction isn’t exactly what your model assumes. If your grasp only works when all those estimates are right, it’s going to be fragile.

So the question is: can we choose a grasp that works across a range of possible conditions? And can we use contact and feedback to correct as we go? Human grasping gives us a very concrete example of the kind of robustness we want robots to have.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty and fragile robot grasps but does not identify humans as susceptible to manipulation errors too.
